passage:
Dear Lokesh,

I have been lying to you for weeks and I hate it. I didn't skip your birthday dinner because of "tuition". I skipped it because Papa's shop has had almost no customers, and I can't afford even the share of the bill. The same with the cricket trip, and the movie. I told everyone I was busy, and I felt like a fraud each time. I was scared you would all look at me differently, or feel sorry for me. Then I saw you looking hurt on Tuesday and thought I owed you the truth. Please don't tell anyone else yet. I'd like to still come to things that cost nothing, like the ground after school. Can we do that?

Shankar

qa.q: Why did Shankar skip Lokesh's birthday dinner?
qa.a: Because Papa's shop has had almost no customers and Shankar could not afford even a share of the bill.

qa.q: Why did Shankar hide the real reason from the friends, and what changed Shankar's mind?
qa.a: Shankar feared being looked at differently or pitied. Seeing Lokesh look hurt made Shankar feel Lokesh was owed the truth.

qa.q: What was wise about Shankar's letter and the request at the end?
qa.a: Shankar chose one trusted friend, stopped pretending, and asked to join things that cost nothing, keeping the friendships without lying or spending money the family doesn't have.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved to know why Shankar kept declining, and perhaps sorry for having been hurt. Lokesh may also feel trusted, and can suggest free plans.

grounding: Shankar hides the family's money trouble out of shame, then tells one trusted friend the truth.

passage:
Hemant, you asked why I always said no to the birthday lunches last year. I'm Maria, and I'll tell you the truth now.
My father lost his job in April. Suddenly there was no money for anything extra. When everyone planned the café lunch for Anjali's birthday, I said I had tuition. For the class trip, I said my grandmother was ill. I made up so many excuses I started forgetting which ones I'd used.
The worst part was how ashamed I felt. Like being short of money made me less.
Once, I even thought about taking the money from Mum's purse, just to go once. I didn't. That scared me though.
Then in October I told Zoe, my best friend. Just her. She said, "Why didn't you say? We'll do a picnic at the park instead, everyone brings something." And she didn't make it weird.
Money isn't who I am. I know that now. I still say no sometimes. But I don't lie about why.

qa.q: When did Maria's father lose his job?
How did Maria feel about the family's money situation?
qa.a: Maria felt deeply ashamed, as if having less money made Maria less of a person.

qa.q: Which steps helped Maria, and why?
qa.a: Telling one trusted friend and stopping the lies, which let friends adjust plans kindly and freed Maria from pretending.

qa.q: How does Zoe react when Maria tells her?
qa.a: Zoe is kind and practical, suggesting a picnic where everyone brings something, and doesn't make it awkward.

grounding: A teen who hid the family's money trouble behind excuses tells one trusted friend, stops pretending and sees money is not the measure of a person.

passage:
Monday. The class planned a trip to the water park. Jaya checked her savings tin at home: nowhere near enough. Since Appa's shop closed, there was nothing extra. At school she said, "I'm busy that day," and changed the subject. Her face burned.
Wednesday. At lunch, someone laughed, "Jaya's always busy." Aadhya, her best friend, saw her look away. On the walk home Aadhya asked quietly, "Is it money?"
Jaya stopped. Her eyes filled. "Yes. I'm tired of lying."
"You don't have to lie to me. You're still you," Aadhya said.
Saturday. Aadhya had asked a few friends to do a free day at the beach instead, packed lunches, frisbee. Nobody asked why. Jaya brought lemon rice. She had thought, for one ugly second, of borrowing money she couldn't pay back. She didn't.
Laughing on the sand, she realised being short of money didn't make her less.

qa.q: Where did the class plan a trip on Monday?
How did Jaya feel when she said she was busy?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and embarrassed, her face burning as she hid the family's money problem.

qa.q: What choice worked for Jaya, and why?
qa.a: Telling Aadhya the truth instead of lying, so a friend could support her and plan a free outing.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see Jaya's situation?
qa.a: Aadhya sees it with kindness, reminding Jaya she is still herself and finding a way for everyone to be together.

grounding: A teen hiding her family's money trouble tells one trusted friend, stops pretending and sees money does not measure her.
